Maxwell's equations govern electromagnetic field interactions and are fundamental to scattering problems.
Conventional numerical methods like MOM, FEM, and FDTD become computationally prohibitive for electrically large scatterers at high frequencies.
The multilevel fast multipole algorithm (MLFMA) reduces computational complexity to O(N log N) but is still costly at very high frequencies.
High-frequency methods exploit ray physics where fields behave like rays following Fermat’s principle and ray tube theory.
Current-based methods include Physical Optics (PO), Physical Theory of Diffraction (PTD), and Incremental Length Diffraction Coefficients (ILDC).
Ray-based methods include Geometric Optics (GO), Geometric Theory of Diffraction (GTD), Uniform Theory of Diffraction (UTD), and Uniform Asymptotic Theory (UAT).
The Numerical Steepest Descent Path (NSDP) method efficiently computes highly oscillatory integrals by contour deformation in the complex plane.
Specular reflection points provide the leading term in scattered fields, while edges and vertices contribute weaker diffracted terms.
The Sommerfeld half-plane problem provides canonical solutions for diffraction from edges.
Creeping waves arise from Fock currents on convex scatterers and decay rapidly along the surface.
The GO method calculates reflected fields with frequency-independent computational workload.
The SBR method combines ray tracing, amplitude tracking, and PO integration to handle multiple reflections and diffractions in complex structures.
GTD diffraction coefficients become singular near shadow boundaries; UTD uses uniform asymptotic expansions to resolve this.
PO induced currents are approximated as twice the cross product of the surface normal and incident magnetic field in lit regions.
The NSDP method allows calculation of PO and ILDC scattered fields with error-controllable accuracy and frequency-independent cost.
The Fresnel transition function describes field behavior near shadow and reflection boundaries.
Uniform asymptotic techniques like Pauli-Clemmow modified steepest descent are used to evaluate diffraction integrals.
The dyadic reflection coefficient for a perfectly conducting scatterer equals a matrix with 1 and -1 on the diagonal for parallel and perpendicular polarizations.
The ray tube technique ensures conservation of energy flux along ray paths.
The ILDC method represents diffracted wave fields as line integrals, while PO scattered fields are surface integrals.
